data.title: While embedding AI 'everywhere,' BNY won't disclose costs
data.description:
• Key insight: BNY, which has leaned heavily into AI in recent years, was reluctant Thursday to say how much it's spending on the technology.
  • What's at stake: Analysts and industry observers are looking for proof that banks' investments in AI will pay off in the form of financial gains.

The Bank of New York Mellon said Thursday that it's embedding artificial intelligence into every corner of its business. What it didn't say is how much money it's spending on AI.
Analysts attempted to extract those details during the custody bank's third-quarter earnings call, but BNY CEO Robin Vince didn't provide a dollar figure. Instead, he talked about the rationale for investing in AI — saying it offers the opportunity to improve outcomes, create capacity and deliver for clients — and arguing that the dollars being spent are generating returns.

The sidestep was hardly surprising. As banks have implemented AI capabilities across their platforms, bank executives have largely deflected analysts' questions about AI-related expenses and returns on investments, saying it's too early in the cycle to provide concrete numbers.

Industry observers have been trying to get a handle on the amount of money that banks are pouring into AI, and whether the investments are producing gains. At BNY, "the answer to the question is yes, we're generating returns, and yes, we want to lean in more," Vince said during the call.

Of BNY's annual $13 billion expense base, about $4 billion is spent on technology, Vince said. 

Regarding the cost of AI specifically, "we're not breaking it out, but it sort of folds into the inputs across our expense base," Vince said. "And frankly, we think it could be counterproductive to break it out and to start obsessing about it publicly and even within the company as an input."

During the bank's second-quarter call in July, Chief Financial Officer Dermot McDonogh offered a slightly meatier response to a question about AI spending. 

"Within the context of $4 billion, AI spend is quite de minimis and quite modest and appropriate for the strategy we have in place," he said at the time.

BNY has championed AI for years. A year ago, it said it had 117 AI solutions in production. That number is now at "400-plus," Vince said Thursday. The bank views AI as a way to increase capacity within its workforce, freeing people up to take care of other tasks, not as a way to reduce headcount, he added.

"We've got plenty of things to do, and so whenever we can generate capacity to provide for that growth without having to grow the expense base, that's phenomenal," Vince said.

Vince's comments followed another strong quarter for the $484 billion-asset bank. It reported firmwide revenues of $5.7 billion, an increase of 12% year over year. Earnings per share totaled $2.34, beating the $2.27 consensus estimate of analysts who were polled by S&P Capital IQ. 

Net income came in at $1.7 billion, up 16% compared with the year-ago quarter. Net interest income rose 15%, primarily as a result of reinvestment of investment securities at higher yields along with balance sheet growth. The increase was partly offset by deposit margin compression. 

Noninterest expenses rose 8% compared with the prior-year quarter to $3.5 billion as of Sept. 30. The company's results included $1 million in provisions for credit losses. The latest return on tangible common equity was 29%, exceeding the medium-term target of 28% that BNY set in January.

Read more

  • Inflation likely to spark more rate hikes: Boston Fed's Collins
  • Why Citi remains cautious on key profitability metric
  • Goldman's Solomon wants 'clear human accountability' on AI
  • BofA says it's ready to 'move forward' after $1.21B penalty

Against the backdrop of positive results, BNY once again made upward revisions to its financial outlook for the year. It now expects 2026 revenue to increase 12%-13%, excluding notable items. It had most recently expected revenue to grow 10%-11% from the prior year. Meanwhile, it expects full-year net interest income to rise 15%, a sharp increase from the 10% previously projected.

BNY also expects expenses to rise between 7%-8% year over year, excluding notable items, mostly as a result of higher revenues. In July, it said full-year expenses were expected to rise 6%-7%, excluding notable items.

During the quarter, BNY repurchased $937 million of common shares and paid out $436 billion in dividends.

data.title: U.S. Bank downsizes mortgages in bid to boost fees, deposits
data.description:
• Key insight: Home loans amounted to about 28% of U.S. Bancorp's total loans on Sept. 30, down from 30% at year end 2025.
  • Expert quote: "Where you get fee revenue, you get deep relationships, you get sticky deposits. That's where we want to extend our balance sheet." — CEO Gunjan Kedia

U.S. Bancorp is growing its loans, and as that expansion unfolds, the composition of its portfolio is changing.

The $703-billion-asset superregional is leaning into commercial real estate, commercial-and-industrial and credit-card loans, viewing those sectors as prime avenues for driving increased deposits and fee income. And as it does so, the relative contribution made by its mortgage-lending operation is expected to shrink over time. The bank's executives also indicated Thursday that auto lending will not be as big an emphasis.

"When we started the year, I believe residential mortgage loans were in the 30% area in terms of loan mix," Chief Financial Officer John Stern told analysts on a call discussing U.S. Bancorp's third-quarter results. "We do see that coming down, more because of the growth in the other categories. We do anticipate mortgages will probably be in the mid-twenties at some point."

U.S. Bancorp, the parent company of U.S. Bank, held $116.8 billion of mortgage loans on Sept. 30. That total amounted to 28% of the Minneapolis-based company's $415.2 billion of total loans. Home loans made up just under 30% of total loans at Dec. 31, 2025.

Card loans, C&I loans and CRE loans give U.S. Bancorp better opportunities to capture fees and deposits, along with spread income, CEO Gunjan Kedia said on the conference call.

"Where you get fee revenue, you get deep relationships, you get sticky deposits. That's where we want to extend our balance sheet," Kedia said.

Stern echoed that point in an interview with American Banker. "We think [the card-C&I-CRE emphasis] is a good usage of the balance sheet," he said. "It can be levered into deposit gathering, as well as fee categories."

Both Kedia and Stern emphasized that U.S. Bancorp has no plans to exit mortgage or auto lending.

"It doesn't mean we give up on mortgage or auto, or anything like that," Stern said in the interview. "We still offer those products. We still think they're an important part of the consumer's life cycle, but it's clear where our focus is."

Another bank's approach

Memphis-based First Horizon Corp.'s pursuit of a similar strategy is taking a more dramatic shape. On Thursday, the $84.3 billion-asset bank announced plans to sell $4.5 billion in consumer mortgages and deploy the capital into higher-yielding loan types, including CRE and C&I loans.

"The intent there was mainly to create capacity on our balance sheet to fund continued growth and investing in longer, deeper relationship opportunities that we see in the marketplace," Bryan Jordan, First Horizon's chairman and CEO, told analysts.

Jordan termed the mortgages First Horizon is selling "essentially non-relationship portfolio assets."

Due to the loan sale, which is expected to close in the fourth quarter, First Horizon reported a third-quarter loss of $94 million. But Jordan said the loan sale would be accretive going forward, as First Horizon converts the proceeds into higher-earning assets.

Third-quarter results

For its part, U.S. Bancorp reported net income totaling $2.2 billion for the quarter ended Sept. 30, up 10% from the same period last year. The company reported record quarterly revenue of $8 billion, driven in large part by a 13% year-over-year increase in fee income, which totaled $3.48 billion. Net interest income increased, too, though at a less-robust 5.6% clip.

Loans totaled $415.2 billion on Sept. 30, up 8.6% from a year earlier. Deposits of $531.7 billion were up 1%.

Capital-markets revenue of $640 million spiked 69% from the third quarter of 2025, boosted by the first full quarter of results from San Francisco-based investment bank BTIG, which U.S. Bancorp acquired June 1.

Credit-card loans totaled $40 billion on Sept. 30, more than an 11% year-over-year increase, reflecting the impact of a new partnership with Amazon. U.S. Bancorp began issuing Amazon's small-business credit cards in May.

Read more:

  • State Street's new wealth-services unit notches early win
  • Solid consumer results at Wells Fargo propel larger profits
  • Impostors got past First Horizon's help desk, suits allege
  • BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering

Credit quality remained solid. Nonperforming loans totaled $1.28 billion on Sept. 30, down 20% from the same time last year. Third-quarter net chargeoffs of $523 million amounted to 0.51% of average loans, down from 0.56% for the third quarter of 2025.
While the company is keeping a watchful eye on asset quality, especially in the wake of the recent interest-rate hike, it hasn't detected any signs of deterioration in either commercial lending or consumer lending, Stern said on the conference call.

Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini described U.S. Bancorp's numbers as "solid." Gerard Cassidy, who covers the bank for RBC Capital Markets, described them as "strong."

Investors appeared to be in a similar frame of mind. Shares in U.S. Bancorp were trading up more than 2% at $57.54 on Thursday afternoon.

data.title: Ohio bank joins credit unions suing Fiserv over security
data.description:
• Key insight: Across the security suits, Fiserv's court filings say stronger login protections are available on many of its systems, and each client decides whether to use them.
  • What's at stake: Fiserv serves about 10,000 financial institutions, and its position puts the job of turning on stronger authentication on those clients.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

A small Ohio bank has become the 10th financial institution represented by the same lawyer to sue Fiserv over its cybersecurity practices. But so far, the suits have made little headway in court.

The suits accuse Fiserv of failing to provide the security it promised, in particular multifactor authentication (a second proof of identity beyond a password) on systems that hold customers' account data. Some also challenge the fees Fiserv charges clients that leave.

The Antwerp Exchange Bank Co. filed the suit Oct. 8 in federal court in Toledo, accusing the core processor of misrepresenting its security to win business from the bank, which has $161 million in assets.

Some of the credit unions asked judges for emergency orders that would force Fiserv to change its practices while their cases proceeded. Courts have denied both such requests a judge has ruled on, but Fiserv has not won outright dismissal of any of the 10 cases.

Fiserv has argued that the lawsuits are about money. By December, it had received 22 demand letters from the same lawyer, Charles Nerko, which it described as substantively identical, according to a filing in Self-Help Credit Union's case.

Self-Help's termination fees "exceed $1.2 million, and Self-Help does not want to pay them," Fiserv said in the same filing.

"Cencap's counsel has sued Fiserv multiple times. Fiserv is familiar with this playbook," the company's lawyers wrote in a June 2025 brief opposing an emergency bid from Cencap Federal Credit Union.

Nerko's clients "openly challenge exit fees, but the security allegations are specific and independently important," he told American Banker.

Nerko has represented financial institutions in all 10 suits since 2018. Antwerp's is the first brought by a bank; credit unions brought the other nine, most recently Marshall Community Credit Union in Michigan, which sued three days before Antwerp did.

Fiserv serves about 10,000 financial institutions, according to its website. Across Nerko's earlier cases, Fiserv has presented courts a consistent position on who is responsible for stronger login protections: Fiserv offers them on many of its systems, and each client decides whether to use them.

"Ultimately, however, the client determines its risk tolerance," Fiserv's lawyers wrote in an Oct. 5 brief opposing an emergency motion from FiCare Federal Credit Union over whether Fiserv's automated call center can lift fraud holds on the credit union's cards.

"We continue to support our clients by implementing security and authentication tools that take into account each of our client's unique needs and preferences," a Fiserv spokesperson told American Banker in a statement Thursday.

Neither Antwerp's complaint nor Marshall's "alleges a specific security incident impacting their customers or data," the spokesperson said. "As with the other suits filed by the same counsel, we believe these claims lack merit and we intend to defend them vigorously in court."

What the bank alleges

Antwerp's complaint rests entirely on trade-secret law: the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and Ohio's version of the same law.

The bank argued that its records of customer identities and accounts are a trade secret. Fiserv got them by misrepresenting its security in the contract and in compliance materials, according to the complaint.

It's a new legal route to the goal all 10 suits share: getting a judge to rule against Fiserv's security practices. Marshall's complaint, filed three days earlier, pairs a trade-secret claim with breach-of-contract and fraud claims. Antwerp's drops those and rests on trade secrets alone.

Fiserv said at a January hearing in Self-Help's case that "nothing in our contract requires us" to adopt NIST's standards.

Indeed, NIST's main catalog of security controls is "mandatory for federal information systems," while private companies are only "encouraged to consider using" it, according to NIST.

Even so, compliance materials Fiserv sends banks say its security practices follow NIST's standards, according to Antwerp's complaint.

Antwerp turned these statements back on Fiserv. If the contract doesn't require Fiserv to follow NIST, then its claims that its security did were "non-contractual statements of fact," the bank argued. "Misrepresentation is an improper means of acquiring a trade secret," the bank said.

The Antwerp complaint lists Fiserv systems that the bank said lack multifactor authentication. Among them is Premier, the core system that holds the bank's customer accounts.

Bank staff log in to Premier with a username, a password and "periodically," an emailed one-time passcode, or OTP, "with an option to use OTP through an authenticator app," according to the complaint.

The complaint argues that a code sent by email doesn't count as a second factor, citing NIST guidelines that bar email for that purpose. It does not say whether the bank uses the authenticator-app option, and Nerko declined to say.

"We do not comment on individual clients' security settings," Nerko said.

Of the nine Fiserv systems the complaint lists, Premier is the only one it describes as offering an authenticator app.

The second factor matters because a bank staff login grants access to customers' account numbers, addresses and Social Security numbers, the complaint said.

The complaint does not describe a specific security incident or fraud loss at the bank. Neither Antwerp's case nor Marshall's depends on showing that one occurred, according to Nerko.

It says Fiserv would demand "seven-figure" fees if the bank left, without giving a figure. Much of its language matches (often word for word) the complaints Marshall and Self-Help filed.

"Banks should not have to pay a vendor's termination-related fees when the vendor does not hold up its end of the bargain," Jeff Mumma, Antwerp's CEO, told American Banker.

Fiserv's answer: The client chose

Fiserv has not yet filed an answer in the Antwerp case, but its defenses in the nine other Nerko cases preview what it is likely to say.

Midwest Family Federal Credit Union "chose not to implement additional security features before or after initiating this action," Fiserv wrote Tuesday in its answer to that Indiana credit union's suit. Nerko represents Midwest in the lawsuit.

Midwest "has refused to migrate to the upgraded authentication method offered by Fiserv, SecureNow," Fiserv said in its answer.

SecureNow adds multifactor authentication to Fiserv's Virtual Branch online banking and Mobiliti mobile banking, according to a July motion Fiserv filed in FiCare's case. Fiserv is replacing its older Enhanced Authentication product with it, according to its answer in the Midwest Family lawsuit.

A Fiserv operations executive took the same position that the bank chooses the security features it uses, under oath in FiCare's case in Florida.

"The financial institution client, not Fiserv, determines whether the client uses OTP" when the call center verifies a cardholder, according to the executive's declaration.

Fiserv's own documents show that it started offering several stronger options only recently.

Authenticator-app passcodes arrived on Portico, a Fiserv core system for credit unions, in June 2025, according to a letter earlier this year from a Fiserv lawyer that Marshall filed as an exhibit.

Multifactor authentication for online-banking enrollment on that core system "became available in April 2025," a Fiserv executive said in a June 2025 declaration in Cencap's case.

CUSA, another Fiserv credit union core, "does not currently support such authentication processes, nor has it ever," the executive said in the same declaration.

The filings do not say when Premier, the core Antwerp uses, gained its authenticator-app option.

The credit unions suing Fiserv object to being pushed onto SecureNow.

Fiserv has said that switching costs extra. Cencap "presumably" decided "the extra security protection was not worth the additional cost of the SecureNow product," Fiserv wrote in the June 2025 brief.

The push to move clients onto SecureNow is "a mid-contract shake-down," according to Midwest's amended complaint.

Fiserv denied that in its answer and said SecureNow "provides additional security capabilities."

The emergency bids

Courts have denied both emergency requests a judge has ruled on in these cases. Neither ruling makes a judgment on whether Fiserv's cybersecurity is adequate; rather, they deny requests asking the judge to order Fiserv to do something, or stop doing something, while the case proceeds.

A federal judge in Connecticut denied an emergency request by Cencap in June 2025, citing the credit union's "years-long unexplained delay in bringing suit," according to the court's order. Cencap had asked the court to bar Fiserv from storing the credit union's information "on any internet accessible system without multi-factor authentication," according to the order.

Self-Help asked a court to make Fiserv cut its Client360 support portal off from the internet and work out a plan for the credit union to leave. A federal judge in North Carolina denied that request in January.

The judge in the Self-Help case noted evidence that the credit union had declined SecureNow "three or more years ago" and said it "has been on notice of the potential problem for a period of time," according to the hearing transcript. Self-Help's emergency bid then fell apart later in the lawsuit.

On April 30, as a penalty for evasive answers, a judge ordered that the credit union be treated as having admitted (among other things) that it could have used authenticator-app passcodes on Portico, the Fiserv core it used, since June 2025.

Its answers to Fiserv's questions were "gamesmanship," the judge said, according to the hearing transcript. The judge ordered Self-Help to pay Fiserv's legal fees for the motion.

The next day, Self-Help withdrew its request for a preliminary injunction, the longer-lasting version of the emergency order it had sought.

It accepted an offer Fiserv had made in January, which let it leave Fiserv later that year without paying termination fees up front. Self-Help withdrew the request based on Fiserv's concessions, according to Nerko.

Bessemer System Federal Credit Union's 2019 request ended in a compromise. Bessemer, which had already left Fiserv, asked the court to stop the company from storing the credit union's records on internet-accessible systems and to hand over records the credit union still needed.

Only FiCare's emergency motion is still pending. It asks the court to stop Fiserv's automated call-center system from lifting fraud holds on FiCare's cards.

Where the cases stand

Fiserv has gotten some procedural wins, but it has not gotten a judge to outright dismiss any of Nerko's 10 lawsuits.

A federal judge in California denied its motion to dismiss Polam Federal Credit Union's suit in June. The issues were better resolved at a later stage of the case, once both sides had gathered evidence, the judge wrote in a two-page order.

In 2020, a federal judge in Pennsylvania let Bessemer's breach-of-contract claim proceed. In 2024, Fiserv and Bessemer agreed to dismiss the case.

A lawsuit by two New York credit unions also settled in 2023, and Cencap's case got dismissed in April after the parties reported a settlement, according to its docket.

Nerko's other seven lawsuits against Fiserv are pending.

data.title: Bill would force bank regulators to disclose Epstein records
data.description:
• Key insight: The Epstein Wall Street Records Act would compel regulatory agencies to publicly release all supervisory records on Jeffrey Epstein and his associates.
  • What's at stake: The legislation targets banks and executives who enabled Epstein, forcing regulators to conduct investigations into potential banking, securities and illicit financing violations.

Democratic lawmakers have introduced a bill that would force federal regulators to investigate banks in connection with Jeffrey Epstein's global sex-trafficking operation, and to publicly disclose related supervisory records.

The Epstein Wall Street Records Act — led by Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — would require financial regulators to identify and penalize financial institutions and bank executives who profited from or ignored red flags while managing Epstein's money. It also mandates that the regulators publicly release all supervisory records and documents related to Epstein's finances and banking activities.

"I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes," Warren said in a press release. "Since they have failed to act, Congress must."

The legislation would require the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission to publicly disclose supervisory records related to Epstein and his associates. 

And it would mandate that those regulators investigate banks and bankers connected to Epstein for possible banking, securities or illicit financing violations. The bill also would mandate that the regulators fine — and bar from the industry — bank executives who assisted Epstein's financial operations. The executives would potentially be referred for criminal violations to the Department of Justice.

The bill has seven sponsors, including one Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and 18 co-sponsors.

Massie was a key figure last year in the fight to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which required the Department of Justice to release documents related to Epstein.

That legislation wasn't initially scheduled for a floor vote in the GOP-controlled House, but Massie was one of four House Republicans who joined Democrats by signing onto a discharge petition, a little-used procedural tactic that can overcome opposition to a vote by the majority party's leaders. 

Ultimately, the 2025 legislation passed the House by a 427-1 vote, and the Senate approved it by unanimous consent. President Trump signed it into law in November.

The Epstein Wall Street Records Act could have an easier path to House passage if Democrats regain control of the chamber, as polls now indicate is likely, in the November elections.

If Democrats win both chambers of Congress and pass the bill, President Trump would have to decide whether to veto it. Such a move could spark a political backlash and lead Congress to override his veto.

"Justice for the survivors means following the money," Massie said in a press release. "The Epstein Wall Street Records Act requires the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the SEC to release their files on Jeffrey Epstein's money." 

Warren released the text of the bill, an explainer and responses from the OCC, the FDIC, and the Fed to her request for investigations into Epstein. Each regulator replied that they cannot disclose nonpublic supervisory information about financial institutions. 

"I cannot confirm the existence of or otherwise comment on specific investigations," Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman wrote in a June 12, 2026, letter to Warren.

Top banks in the crosshairs of the Epstein scandal include JPMorganChase, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America, each of which were cited in an August report by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee. On Thursday, Warren publicly released letters from Barclays, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan, responding to her questions this summer about Epstein and specific bankers.  

Kathleen Mellody, head of federal government relations at JPMorgan, said in the company's letter to Warren that the New York bank ended its relationship with Epstein in 2013. CEO Jamie Dimon "never met Jeffrey Epstein, never emailed him, and was not involved in any decision to have him as a client," she wrote. 

"JPMC shares the view that Jeffrey Epstein's acts were reprehensible," Mellody wrote. "The firm did not facilitate or knowingly enable illegal activity." 

Wyden's report on Epstein listed 13 senior bankers at JPMorgan, BofA and Deutsche who allegedly protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black, the former CEO of private equity giant Apollo Global Management, who made $170 million in payments to Epstein.The report details how the three banks retroactively flagged thousands of questionable financial transactions after the notorious sex offender's death in 2019. Epstein died in prison after his arrest on sex-trafficking charges.

Garcia, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, summed up the Democrat's intentions going forward. 

"We need to know what financial institutions and their executives knew about Epstein, whether they complied with relevant law, and what regulatory agencies learned," Garcia said in the press release. 

JPMorgan, Deutsche and BofA all declined to comment.

data.title: Maybe inflation isn't such a big problem after all
data.description:
Inflation? What inflation?
On the election trail, inflation is such a big issue that it may on its own lead to a change in power in Washington, D.C. In the markets, inflation is such a big deal that the pronouncements of every Fed official, even the rank and file ones who are setting policy, make headlines. But in the real world, maybe inflation isn't that big a deal?

I know that last statement feels wrong. The cost of virtually everything these days is noticeably higher, and it has people in a foul mood. I myself get anxiety every time I check out at the grocery store; it feels like I can't get out of there without dropping at least $100. On that level, inflation is definitely an issue, and an acute one. 

And inflation is accelerating, again. On Wednesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the August consumer price index rose, showing inflation running at a 3.7% annual rate. That is up from July, and not the direction you want if you're a central banker, a president, or anybody really. The report sparked chatter that the Fed was going to be forced to raise rates at its next FOMC meeting in a couple of weeks. 

But if you look at the first clutch of earnings reports from the nation's biggest banks, inflation does not seem to be having much effect on their P&Ls at all, even when you're looking at how their retail businesses are faring. 

Client balances at Citi's wealth division, which now includes its retail bank, rose 9% in the third quarter compared to a year ago, rising to $1.4 trillion. The unit's revenue rose 15% and income 93%. Maybe you could argue the bulk of that came from wealthier clients less affected by inflation.

At Well Fargo, both revenue and profit rose on the back of two completely consumer-driven activities: people taking out new credit-card accounts and auto loans. The bank said it saw strength among its clients across income levels and  that its nonaccrual consumer loan level fell 8% from a year ago, certainly not a sign of rising stress. 

JPMorganChase, which earned a cool $15 billion in the third quarter, said net chargeoffs in its consumer and community banking operations were flat from a year ago at $1.98 billion. Its overall provision for credit losses fell to $2.7 billion from $3.4 billion a year ago (albeit up a bit from $2.5 billion a quarter ago).

I do think there are real issues that people are facing, but those issues don't appear to be hurting banks, not yet at least. At the very least that means people are still spending and taking on credit, which should result in the economy continuing to grow to some degree.

The risks of consumer AI 
I'll tell you honestly, I don't even like to give my doctor information about my health. I don't like to tell my bank about my money, and they are holding my money. I do these things, of course, but I'm not comfortable about doing them. I was wired at a time when you didn't just hand out details about your life to whoever asked. 

My attitude is definitely an anachronism, and it is only going to get more anachronistic as time goes on, because now you can tell your entire life to a chatbot and then ask it to do things for you. "Agentic AI," they call it, in case you haven't heard. But holding all that information, and doing things with it, comes with responsibilities, not only for the consumers and tech companies running the bots, but for banks as well. 

JPMorgan executives talked a lot during their third-quarter conference call about the risks of people using AI agents, and what competitive risks that creates for banks. The fear is that chatbots will ruthlessly search out the best rates and create a lot of competition for deposits among banks.

But there's another issue for banks, a very real legal issue that needs to be ironed out, our Kate Berry reports. If banks use AI agents themselves, say for customer service, they could break consumer-protection laws depending on what the bot does, or doesn't let the customer do, with a customer's information, a new study warned.

In essence, whoever controls the chatbot, and let's say that's your bank, is responsible for every action of that chatbot, every answer given, every dead end arrived at, every roadblock hit or promise broken. It is a wide Sargasso Sea of uncertainty, and banks are going to have to either game out all of it beforehand or wade through it in real time.

data.title: BankThink A TradFi veteran reflects on one year working in digital assets
data.description:
• Key insight: Digital assets and artificial intelligence-driven agents are going to transform financial services, and the change is going to happen in a hurry. The industry can take some key steps to weather the transition.
  • What's at stake: Both AI agents and digital assets are transformative technologies on their own, but coming together as they are now, they will bring an accelerated level of change that neither technology could have achieved on its own.
  • Forward look: The whole ecosystem of players must lean in and collaborate to ensure legal, regulatory and compliance safeguards are in place, and that the potential of the new technology is fully achieved to benefit our clients and industry.

It is becoming increasingly clear that digital assets are poised to reshape financial services in ways many of us may underestimate.

As a payments and transaction banking professional who has spent the past 18 months immersed in the digital assets space, I have been thinking about the transformational impact of digital assets for the financial services industry — trying to think beyond the hype. My reflections are based on many conversations with peers and partners. They are also based on client needs, market dynamics and business economics. I come at these reflections with decades of experience that combine traditional banking, working at a fintech, and consulting to banks and large corporates.

In all my years working with clients I have not felt this level of optimism for what we can finally deliver to clients in terms of breadth of solutions, sophistication of capabilities, ease of access, degree of availability and removal of friction. However, living up to that promise will require the financial services industry to be both ambitious and thoughtful, driven and collaborative, visionary and pragmatic. Most importantly, we will need to remain focused on the client and how new innovations will best meet their needs and goals.

In a three-part series, I explore how digital assets may reshape financial services. I recognize it is early in the journey, and things may play out in numerous ways. However, I believe structural shifts that will shape our industry are already emerging.

Here are five ways that things may play out for the financial services industry, summarized here and further explored in the next two parts of the series.

Digital assets are fundamentally reshaping banking and financial services at a faster pace and to a greater degree than we expect because of the combination of agentic AI and tokenization. Both AI agents and digital assets are transformative technologies on their own, but coming together as they are now, they will bring an accelerated level of change that neither technology could have achieved on its own. The growth of agentic AI will drive transaction paths that are programmable, always-on and frictionless. In parallel, the promise of tokenization of both money and real-world assets require end-to-end processes that are fully tokenized, which, in turn, will create pressure to innovate faster. The combination of these two market forces creates a double flywheel effect, which will generate urgency and incentives for financial transactions that are simpler, faster, cheaper, always-on and frictionless.

Read more:

  • FDIC's Hill cites 'more work to do' on tokenized deposits
  • Crypto comes to rescue vulnerable House banking Republicans
  • Bankers grapple with liability when AI agents mess up
  • Earnings Goldman's Solomon wants 'clear human accountability' on AI

Clients may not specifically ask their banks for digital assets products, but they do want simple, programmable, and intelligent ways to manage money and real-world assets. Once clients see what's possible, there will be no putting the genie back in the bottle. These capabilities will increasingly become the standard and shape client expectations and needs. The role of product management is not to react to client asks and self-diagnoses, but rather to understand current and future client goals in order to deliver solutions the client hasn't even considered. The institutions that can translate new technology into meaningful client value, before the client even asks for it, will be best positioned to win.
Digital assets are both a product and a rail, but this is not (just) about infrastructure, it is a paradigm shift in how financial services will be delivered, managed and consumed. Tokenization will shift business and revenue models, drive changes in client behavior and expectations, and redefine key concepts in financial services such as trust and money. The transformation occurring in the industry is not only reshaping the infrastructure, it is also reshaping the client experience. Thinking about tokenization in terms of improved products or rails limits us in our ability to imagine a future that is vastly different from what we have now. While it may be relatively easy to understand immediate and visible benefits of new technology, it is nearly impossible to imagine what it will be in the future after multiple compounded innovation hops. If history is any guide, we cannot fully anticipate how profoundly tokenization will reshape the industry.

It is risky for the incumbents to take a "do nothing" or "wait and see" approach. At the same time, the industry needs to ensure it is embracing the new technology and business models in a way that keeps the client and their needs at the center of everything we do. Previous waves of innovation have shown that incumbent institutions are often best positioned to succeed, provided they are willing to disrupt themselves before clients or competitors force them to do so. But there is also a risk that we get too enamored with the technology and forget to articulate the problems we are solving for clients — and why solving them is important. Collaboration is also critical to innovation, including participation in industry consortia and initiatives. Key to success for the incumbents will be the willingness to be an early mover, an unwavering focus on clients, and the ability to operationalize partnerships and networks. Those who do that will have disproportionate gains.

The financial services industry will need to get two things right in order to enable client adoption at scale and achieve the full benefits: (i) a minimum viable ecosystem of banks, fintechs, counterparties, infrastructure providers, and systems; and (ii) the legal, ethical and regulatory frameworks to address failures, disputes, and unintended consequences. Mass adoption will only happen if we have distribution and reach without added friction and fragmentation and frameworks to address consumer protection, identity management, proof of intent, liability, and accountability. While the technology is important, perhaps more important is the ability to overcome the innovation challenges that are not related to technology. Success will require focus on collaboration and a willingness to create a shared ecosystem, as well as the ability to create a financial service system that is fair, transparent, explainable, predictable and consistent.

Ultimately, while the details and nuances may evolve differently from what I have laid out, I believe that digital assets are reshaping financial services at a greater pace and magnitude than many of us expected just a year or two ago. The whole ecosystem of players must lean in and collaborate to ensure legal, regulatory and compliance safeguards are in place, and that the potential of the new technology is fully achieved to benefit our clients and industry. At stake is our ability to deliver financial services to clients in a way that is simpler, more accessible and more effective.

data.title: Banks face liability over use of AI chatbots, report finds
data.description:
• Key insight: When banks use AI chatbots to provide customer support on decisions about mortgages and loans, they can risk violating consumer-protection laws.
  • Supporting data: Corporations remain liable when chatbots give wrong answers, create endless doom loops, or fail to solve problems, former regulators argue in  a new report. 

Banks that use AI agents for customer service may be breaking consumer-protection laws if the technology makes decisions impacting a customer's finances or blocks a consumer from getting help, according to a new report by former regulators.

"If something is illegal or unlawful, the fact that a chatbot does it isn't a shield from liability," said Adam Teitelbaum, a former director of consumer protection at the Office of the Attorney General for the District of Columbia, and a co-author of the study.

Teitelbaum and his co-author, Stephanie Nguyen, a former chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission, are pressing for more enforcement at the state level amid the Trump administration's retreat from enforcing consumer-protection laws.

"Given the scale and speed of how these technologies are being deployed, what's happening is we're seeing in real time how people are being impacted like guinea pigs in an experiment," Nguyen said.

Using consumers as a testbed for unproven AI systems has created a massive, systemic breakdown, Nguyen argued. When companies deploy AI chatbots as intermediaries, they are responsible for every false answer, dead end, roadblock and broken promise, she added. 

The study identifies false information as one of three areas in which misconduct by chatbots could trigger state bans for unfair and deceptive practices.  Those agents have shown repeatedly they can "hallucinate" and go rogue, routinely providing false or misleading information. 

AI chatbots also can obstruct consumers' access to a live human being, and they may provide an inadequate service that fails to solve a customer's problem. In addition to enforcement actions at the state level, individual consumers harmed by chatbot failures can pursue lawsuits under state consumer-protection statutes.

"AI chatbot" is a general term used by the study's co-authors to encompass everything from automated voice assistance to AI-enabled help to any automated chatbot on websites, apps and search engines.

Amid the rapid spread of this technology, financial institutions and vendors to banks and fintechs are actively seeking to manage their downside risks. But banks and fintechs face a delicate balancing act in managing AI compliance while staying competitive. Some financial firms are seeking guidance from regulators because operating without regulatory standards creates legal risks, experts say.

"If you're doing something to manage your risk, and you think that's right, but a competitor is willing to take more risk, that can yield outcomes that put [a company] at a financial disadvantage," said Benjamin Saul, a partner at the law firm Steptoe.

Banks are quick to differentiate between agentic AI and AI chatbots that are based on machine-learning and are widely used in banking. Small, midsize and regional banks have largely been cautious about using agentic AI at scale in customer service because of the need for ongoing oversight.

At large banks, however, AI chatbots increasingly rely on both machine learning and agentic AI to handle complex work with minimal human involvement. For example, Bank of America's virtual assistant Erica, which has handled more than 3.2 million customer interactions, is a hybrid system that is built on machine-learning but has evolved to perform agentic AI functions, experts said.

"Corporations cannot hide behind AI to dodge accountability," said Teitelbaum, who is currently a senior fellow at the nonprofit Protect Borrowers. He and Nguyen are urging policymakers to mandate that companies give customers the option of immediately connecting to a human being in a single click.

At the state level, the Conference of State Bank Supervisors released an AI supervisory framework last month that provides specific instructions for examiners to evaluate financial institutions. State officials have subpoena authority to audit internal AI model code as well as examine complaint logs to enforce existing consumer-protection statutes. 

"State attorneys general are on the front lines," said Teitelbaum. "They already have the investigative tools to look under the hood of these systems — and the authority to hold companies accountable when their chatbots fail."

Read more:

  • Inflation likely to spark more rate hikes: Boston Fed's Collins
  • Why Citi remains cautious on key profitability metric
  • Goldman's Solomon wants 'clear human accountability' on AI
  • BofA says it's ready to 'move forward' after $1.21B penalty

As for federal oversight, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., expressly excluded agentic AI from interagency model risk management guidance that was revised in April. However, the prudential regulators still expect banks to maintain strong compliance and risk-management programs when using AI, experts said.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has largely halted enforcement under the Trump administration. It has issued past guidance requiring a bank or creditor that uses machine learning or complex AI algorithms to provide a specific reason to an applicant who was denied credit. 

Customer service has been a compliance focal point for many years. Historically, companies have used what the industry calls "phone tree loops" and moved workers offshore to cut costs.

"This is just the next evolution of the customer-service function," said Teitelbaum. "Providing a service that you've promised customers can sometimes be expensive, and it can sometimes save your bottom line by keeping people from being able to cancel a service quickly because a lot of people are just going to give up."
